reasoning.reasoning: An appointment slot is perishable capacity, so a no-show with no fee costs you the whole slot because it's too late to rebook it — which means the absent customer pays nothing while you eat the idle coordinator time, and without a deposit there's no incentive keeping the calendar honest.
reasoning.conclusion: Require a card-on-file deposit or a {x}% late-cancel fee on booking bookings, waived only with {x}h notice so the slot can be resold.
reasoning.expected_effect: Recovering even half the no-show slots is worth ~${x}/mo in otherwise-dead capacity.

title: A missing rung in your price ladder

reasoning.observation: Your menu item prices cluster at {x} points with a gap of ${x} between tiers — customers either trade down hard or balk at the jump.
reasoning.reasoning: A ladder with a missing rung loses two groups at once: value seekers with no entry below the cluster, and would-be trade-ups facing too big a leap to the premium. The gap caps both your floor traffic and your mix-up potential.
reasoning.conclusion: Introduce one menu item at the missing price point (good-better-best), positioned to catch the trade-up rather than discount the existing tier.
reasoning.expected_effect: Filling the rung captures both lost trade-downs and easier trade-ups, ~${x}/mo in mix.

reasoning.reasoning: Churn is cheapest to fix early: a customer slowing down still remembers you, so an intervention now costs far less than reacquiring them later at full walk_in acquisition cost.
reasoning.conclusion: Trigger a graduated win-back on the at-risk segment — a personal walk_in touch before a discount — rather than waiting for them to fully lapse.
reasoning.expected_effect: Catching even a fraction of pre-churn customers protects ~${x}/mo in retained round revenue.

swarm_upgrade: CustomerJourneyAgent + RFMAgent: stitch a durable per-customer history by resolving identity across transactions ↔ anonymous_customer_profiles ↔ customer_sessions ↔ caller_memory_index (loyalty id / phone / card token / session fingerprint), then compute recency-frequency-monetary per customer. Walk-in transactions are largely identity-less today, so this must be built before the insight can fill. ChurnPredictAgent (on top of CustomerJourneyAgent/RFMAgent): model lapse probability and the leading pre-churn behavior pattern from the stitched per-customer history; emits an at-risk score and an intervention window.

reasoning.reasoning: A manual reorder is a churn opportunity every cycle; a subscription converts a recurring need into locked recurring revenue and removes the competitor's window between purchases.
reasoning.conclusion: Offer subscription at the moment of a repeat purchase — auto-replenish on the items customers already rebuy on a cadence — rather than as a generic signup.
reasoning.expected_effect: Converting habitual rebuyers to subscription is worth ~${x}/mo in locked recurring visits.

Plus SubscriptionAgent to detect a per-customer replenishment cadence on the same SKU vs. existing subscription enrollment.

reasoning.reasoning: Retention marketing only works on customers you can contact, so an unreachable base caps every win-back, loyalty, and reactivation play before it starts — the gap isn't the message, it's that the channel to deliver it was never captured, which silently ceilings the return on all downstream retention spend.
reasoning.conclusion: Collect opt-in contact at the point of cover (tied to a receipt, loyalty perk, or rebook) and set a {x}% capture-rate target for the attendant at checkout.
reasoning.expected_effect: Lifting contactable share by {x} points expands the addressable base for ~${x}/mo of retainable revenue.

swarm_upgrade: ConsentAgent: contact presence + marketing-consent flags exist on customer profiles, so contactable share is measurable; tying it to the full transacting base still needs CustomerJourneyAgent + RFMAgent: stitch a durable per-customer history by resolving identity across transactions ↔ anonymous_customer_profiles ↔ customer_sessions ↔ caller_memory_index (loyalty id / phone / card token / session fingerprint), then compute recency-frequency-monetary per customer. Walk-in transactions are largely identity-less today, so this must be built before the insight can fill.

title: Personal-occasion triggers (birthday/anniversary) go unused

reasoning.observation: {x}% of customers have a known birthday/anniversary on file, but only {x}% receive any occasion-timed outreach.
reasoning.reasoning: An occasion is a built-in reason to return that the customer already welcomes, so an birthday/anniversary-timed offer converts far better than a generic blast because it lands exactly when intent is naturally high — leaving these triggers unworked forfeits the cheapest, most-welcome touch in the calendar.
reasoning.conclusion: Trigger an automated birthday/anniversary offer via walk_in timed to each customer's date, and reactivate lapsed customers with the same hook.
reasoning.expected_effect: Occasion-timed outreach lifts repeat drinks for ~${x}/mo at near-zero cost.

Plus a LifecycleAgent to store each customer's occasion date (birthday/anniversary/recall-due) and schedule the timed trigger — occasion dates are not captured at acquisition today.

title: People see the wait and leave without ever lining up

title: A full store turns people away at your busiest minute

reasoning.observation: When occupancy nears the {x}-person cap, vision shows door entries flatten or dip even though passerby volume is still rising.
reasoning.reasoning: At the very moment demand peaks, visible crowding/queuing deters new entrants — the store self-limits its own throughput. This is a capacity-shaped revenue ceiling distinct from conversion: the lost customers never even enter, so no in-store fix can recover them; only faster turnover or relieved density can.
reasoning.conclusion: Increase throughput at the cap (expedite checkout, second service point, clear the entry) so occupancy turns over instead of saturating during the {x} peak.
reasoning.expected_effect: Each relieved peak hour recaptures ~{x} suppressed entries (~${x}/mo).

title: Your busiest daypart converts worst

reasoning.observation: The {x} daypart pulls your highest footfall but converts {x}pts below the quieter {x} daypart.

title: Your online menu/listing is stale — orders fail at checkout

reasoning.observation: {x}% of online drink attempts hit an out-of-stock, wrong-price, or unavailable item, and {x}% of those sessions abandon without reordering.
reasoning.reasoning: An online listing is the only salesperson on your highest-potential channel, so when it shows items you don't have or prices you don't honor the customer's trust breaks at the worst moment — at checkout — and because a failed online order rarely converts to a phone call, that demand leaks straight to a competitor whose listing is accurate.
reasoning.conclusion: Sync the online catalog to live availability and pricing, set a weekly listing audit, and flag out-of-stock items in real time so customers never select what you can't fulfill.
reasoning.expected_effect: Eliminating failed-listing aborts recovers ~${x}/mo of online drinks that currently abandon at checkout.

reasoning.expected_effect: Capturing the affinity-driven attach is worth ~${x}/mo at the same traffic.

reasoning.reasoning: Unlike a void, a refund moves money back out the door, so an elevated refund rate is real cash erosion — and refunds keyed to cash (not the card that paid) are a textbook diversion pattern distinct from genuine job returns. The break is abrupt rather than a slow drift — check it before approving any further refunds.
reasoning.conclusion: Reconcile each refund over ${x} to its original tender, and flag any refund issued to a tender that differs from the sale.
reasoning.expected_effect: Reining the rate back to baseline recovers ~${x}/mo of leaked cash.

swarm_upgrade: AnomalyLedgerAgent: ingest refund events with original-tender linkage so refunds keyed to a different tender than the sale can be flagged. Current swarm has aggregate revenue only.

title: Your regulars aren't being recognized as regulars

reasoning.observation: {x}% of drinks are from repeat customers, yet there's no cue to recognize them at the barista or remember their preferences.
reasoning.reasoning: Recognition is the cheapest loyalty lever there is — a returning customer treated like a stranger loses the relationship premium that made them valuable, while a remembered preference deepens it.
reasoning.conclusion: Surface a returning-customer cue and last-visit preference at point of service so regulars feel known.
reasoning.expected_effect: Recognizing regulars lifts repeat frequency and is worth ~${x}/mo in deepened loyalty.

swarm_upgrade: RepeatPurchaseAgent: surface a returning-customer flag + last-visit preference at point of service from transaction history.

reasoning.expected_effect: Active review response lifts conversion of review-readers, worth ~${x}/mo in new drinks.
